crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Predicting proposal success is the use of data and models to estimate whether a grant application will be funded, often before or during review. It sits in grant proposals and funding, where program officers, research development staff, and principal investigators want to triage effort and understand reviewer priorities. The topic overlaps with bibliometrics, peer review studies, and science of science research. The World of AI library holds 135 research papers and 13109 claims extracted from research works, which can support a structured review of what is known.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on historical grant records, award abstracts, reviewer comments, and administrative data, joined with publication and citation histories where available. Most pipelines use Python or R for tabular modeling and natural language processing, with SQL databases for storage and querying. Training large language models may need GPUs, but simpler logistic regression and gradient boosted trees run on ordinary CPUs. Data access is often the limiting factor, because funders and institutions control proposal text and review scores.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common approach defines a binary or ordinal outcome, such as funded or not funded, reviewer score, or funding percentile. Features are drawn from the proposal text, the applicant's publication and funding history, the institution, the team, the budget, and the fit to the funder's stated priorities. Models range from logistic regression and gradient boosted trees to transformer based text classifiers, and they are validated on later grant cycles to avoid leaking future information. Evaluation looks at discrimination, calibration, and whether the model identifies proposals that reviewers would also rank highly. Because peer review is noisy and funding decisions depend on panel dynamics and budgets, predictions are best treated as uncertain signals rather than verdicts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Proposal text, reviewer comments, and administrative records are often confidential, so use requires clear rights, consent, or a legal basis, and provenance must be documented from source to model. Risks include reproducing historical funding disparities by institution, career stage, discipline, or demographic group, and creating feedback loops that favor proposals similar to past winners. Models can also be gamed if applicants learn what features score well, which may penalize unconventional ideas. Good practice includes data minimization, access controls, versioned datasets, model cards, and human review before any funding decision. This page describes practice and is not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Future work is likely to combine text models with structured data from funder systems, so predictions update as a proposal moves through review. Retrieval and summarization tools may help program staff find relevant expertise and check fit, while portfolio level models could estimate the effect of funding decisions across a field. Progress will depend on access to linked, longitudinal data and on shared benchmarks that respect confidentiality. The topic will remain contested because peer review is a social process, and a model that predicts current outcomes may not predict what a funder should support.
